newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Stet to hunt for foreign partners.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Stet to hunt for foreign partners.

text.p: Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, fresh from unveiling a shake-up of telecoms holding Stet, was quoted on Sunday as saying the group was now on the lookout for strong international partners.
"The group needs to find solid and strong alliances in world markets," Ciampi told Il Sole 24 Ore in an interview.

Although Stet has a Wall Street listing and is one of the biggest telecommunications groups in the world, it has been slow to forge a coherent international strategy and analysts say it needs to establish itself in Europe as a powerful force.

The Treasury abruptly announced on Friday a reshuffle of Stet's top managers and outlined details of a merger between the holding and its main operating subsidiary Telecom Italia as a prelude to its long-delayed privatisation.

The Treasury, seeking to inject new blood and show it was serious about a swift privatisation, appointed Telecom Italia director-general Tomaso Tommasi di Vignano in place of Stet managing director Ernesto Pascale.
Chairman Biagio Agnes was replaced by Guido Rossi, who led industrial giant Ferruzzi out of crisis in the mid-1990s.

The announcements, after the market close on Friday, have sparked a storm from opposition politicians who say the government has packed Stet with its own people. Prime Minister Romano Prodi has shrugged off the criticism.
All eyes will be on how the shares fare on Monday morning. Stet closed 107 lire ($0.67) lower on Friday at 7,883 and Telecom Italia was 122 lire weaker at 4,543.
"I think it's positive," said one senior stockbroker who declined to be named. "Hopefully it will send a signal to the market that this privatisation is finally going to happen."

Both companies hold board meetings on Thursday and are expected to give the green light to the fusion, which will create a "supergroup", to be called Telecom Italia, with a market capitalisation of some 55 trillion lire.
The meetings are also set to begin the process of working out how Stet shares will be distributed to Telecom Italia shareholders.
Full details of the merger are expected to be decided by the end of August and the sale, already dubbed the "mother of all privatisations", is expected to take place by October.
The sell-off was slated for last year but the government reluctantly postponed it after political bickering delayed the creation of a watchdog body to oversee the privatised sector.

Legislation to create the watchdog is still blocked in parliament and a key government ally, the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, has threatened to topple the government if the sale goes ahead.

Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said on Saturday his party remained opposed. "Our position, on which we will fight, is that the majority of shares should stay in state hands," he said.

Il Sole said the Treasury, which recently took over control of Stet from heavily-indebted industrial holding group IRI and owns just over 60 percent, was likely to fix a two to three percent ceiling on shareholdings.
That would prevent a predator from building up a big stake.
Il Sole noted that the state's holding in the enlarged group would fall to around 45 percent after the Telecom-Stet merger. ($1=1597 Lire)
